newsitem.title: INDIA: India bourse stresses need for retail investors.
newsitem.headline: India bourse stresses need for retail investors.

text.p: Indian stock markets must win back the confidence of badly wounded retail investors who are running for cover in low-risk investments, the chief of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) said.
"Bringing back retail investors is the key to reviving the markets," BSE president Madan Gopal Damani told Reuters after a news conference late on Tuesday.
During the news conference, Damani said he would suggest ways to rebuild confidence in Indian stock markets during a meeting with Finance Minister P. Chidambaram next week.

Damani said his suggestions would include a compulsory audit of the end-use of funds raised in the capital market, a quarterly disclosure of company accounts, disciplinary action against stock issuers with unsound financial plans and the blocking of issues by these companies.
The BSE had seen market capitalisation decline from 5,943 billion rupees to 4,503 billion from the time of India's annual budget announcement on July 22 to October 4, Damani said.
He said some 50 percent of a total 6,690 scrips listed on the Bombay bourse were trading below par. Only around 2,600 were traded daily with the number falling every day.
"I think we have a crisis looming on the horizon," he said. More than 25 million retail investors trade on India's 23 stock exchanges.
Damani said the BSE would evaluate new issues and may decide to deny listing to issues which were not up to the mark. He said other stock exchanges across the country were also likely to co-operate.
BSE member broker Sunil Shah said during the Tuesday news conference the percentage of national savings invested in financial assets had dropped to around 10 percent from 17.5 percent in 1984.
"We are seeing a reversal of the equity cult. People don't buy shares any more and that's the bottom line," Shah said.

The benchmark Bombay stocks index has fallen some 18 percent since July 22 and brokers say measures introduced in Chidambaram's budget, including the imposition of a 12.9 percent minimum tax on previously untaxed company profits, have hit the markets.
The index was trading 16.06 points higher at 3135.01 in afternoon trade on Wednesday.

Other factors responsible for the decline in share prices are tight credit in late 1995 and political worries in the run-up to general elections earlier this year which have resulted in a slower industrial growth rate in the first half of 1996/97 (April-March).
Returns on investments in equities fell sharply after companies began taking advantage of free pricing of initial public offerings in 1993 to issue shares at inflated prices.
"Investors have seen their hard-earned money simply disappearing into thin air," Shah said.
He said investors saw no reason to put money in equity markets when they were getting a relatively risk free return of upto 18.5 percent in debt issues.
"I think we have a crisis looming on the horizon," he said.
